html:
The Guanches were the native people of the Canary Islands, in the Atlantic off Morocco, before the Spanish conquest. Strictly the name belongs to the people of Tenerife, but it is used for all the islanders. On this map they appear in 1492, the year Columbus stopped in the Canaries on his way west.

Their ancestors came from North Africa, probably in the 1st millennium BCE, and spoke a language related to the Berber languages. They lived by herding goats and sheep and by growing barley, which they toasted and ground into gofio. They had no metal and made tools of stone and obsidian. Many lived in caves. Each island developed on its own, ruled by local kings called menceys on Tenerife.

The conquest of the Canary Islands took almost a century, from 1402 to 1496, first under Norman adventurers for Castile and then under Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand. Tenerife held out longest, and its warriors defeated the Spanish at Acentejo in 1494. Many Guanches were killed, enslaved or died of disease. The survivors mixed with the settlers, and their language died out in the 17th century. The islands became a stepping stone for Columbus and the Spanish Atlantic.
